lessons.title: Planning and organising the maintenance programme
lessons.html:
From schedule to programme

At N4 level the focus was on knowing assets and keeping schedules. At N5 level the manager plans and organises a full maintenance programme: deciding priorities, allocating people and workshop capacity, controlling spares and costs, and fitting maintenance around the farming calendar.

Setting priorities

Not every asset deserves the same attention. Rank assets by criticality:

CriticalityCriteriaExamples
HighFailure stops production, harms animals, or creates a safety or legal riskMilking machine, borehole pump in dry season, harvester in harvest, sprayer calibration
MediumFailure causes delays but there are alternativesSecond tractor, slasher
LowFailure has little impactGarden equipment, spare trailer

High-criticality assets get preventive and condition-based maintenance, critical spares held in stock and a contingency plan such as a standby pump or a contractor on call.

The annual maintenance calendar

Overlay the maintenance tasks on the production calendar. Major work is scheduled in slack periods; pre-season inspections are timed so that parts can still be ordered. For a summer grain and cattle farm: overhaul planters and sprayers in winter; service harvesters before May; check firebreaks and fire equipment before the winter fire season; inspect handling facilities before weaning and pregnancy testing.

Organising resources

  • People – identify who does what: operators (daily care), farm mechanic (services, minor repairs), dealers and specialists (warranty, electronics, major overhauls).
  • Workshop – adequate space, lifting equipment, tools, compressor, welding equipment and a safe layout with fire protection.
  • Information – manuals, parts books, service history and a planner showing jobs due.

Work orders

Use a work-order or job-card system so every task is requested, approved, scheduled, completed and signed off. Open work orders are reviewed weekly so nothing is forgotten.

lessons.title: Controlling maintenance costs and spares
lessons.html:
Understanding maintenance costs

Maintenance costs include parts and materials, own labour, contractor fees, lubricants and the cost of downtime. Downtime cost is often the largest and the least visible: a harvester standing for three days in a wet season may mean grain losses and quality downgrades worth far more than the repair.

Recording and analysing costs

Cost every job card and post it to the asset. Each season, summarise per asset:

  • Total repair and maintenance cost.
  • Cost per hour of use (repair cost divided by hours worked).
  • Number of breakdowns and total downtime.

Example: tractor A cost R96,000 in repairs over 1,200 hours (R80 per hour); tractor B cost R54,000 over 1,500 hours (R36 per hour). Tractor A warrants investigation: is it older, misused, or due for replacement?

Repair or replace?

As an asset ages, repair costs per hour usually rise and reliability falls. Consider replacement when:

  • Repair costs per hour rise steeply or a major overhaul approaches the value of the machine.
  • Downtime threatens critical operations.
  • Newer equipment offers clear savings in fuel, labour or timeliness.
  • Safety standards are no longer met.

A partial budget comparing keeping and replacing the asset helps support the decision.

Controlling spares and stores

  • Keep a stock list with minimum and re-order levels for fast-moving items (filters, belts, bearings, shear bolts, drippers).
  • Hold critical spares for high-criticality assets, especially where lead times from suppliers are long.
  • Issue parts only against a job card so use is traced to an asset.
  • Do regular stock counts and investigate shortages.
  • Avoid tying up too much money in slow-moving stock.

Maintenance budget

Base next year's budget on history per asset, adjusted for planned overhauls, new assets and price increases. Monitor actual against budget monthly.

Key points

  • Rank assets by criticality and focus effort on high-criticality items.
  • Fit major maintenance into slack periods of the production calendar.
  • Use work orders and cost every job to the asset.
  • Use cost per hour and downtime to guide repair-or-replace decisions.
  • Control spares with re-order levels and issue only against job cards.
